title: Feedback sprint brief — priority coffers (sep 2025)
body:
Purpose:
A compact working brief for the fast feedback sprint (Sep 2025). Goal = condense raw signals from support, SRE telemetry, and product interviews into a prioritized set of customer-facing patches / small features we can ship in 2–8 weeks, plus one experimental spike.

Quick snapshot:
- Signals ingested: ~82 tickets (support), 12 in-product telemetry anomalies, 9 customer interviews (CS-led), 3 SRE incidents referenced.
- Primary user personas: platform-engineers (dedicated/private), ML engineers (model serving, quantization), and product engineers (hosted-api integrations).
- Most-cited pain: unpredictability of tail latency and surprising token-cost blowups on short bursts of long-context traffic.

Cross-cutting themes (synth):
1) Latency variability for long-context requests
   - Pattern: customers running chat histories or long-document prompts (~8k+ tokens) see intermittent 2–6x latency spikes. Appears correlated with cache warmup and fallback to single-request kernels.
   - Impact: user-facing timeouts, increased error rates, pushes teams to reduce context length -> quality regression.

2) KV / prefix-cache mismatch and token-duplication artifacts
   - Pattern: several customers report repeated tokens or partial duplication when cache gets out-of-sync across replicas after scaled rollouts. Often triggered after rapid canary increases or model-variant fallbacks.
   - Impact: non-deterministic outputs impair production customers with strict output SLAs.

3) Limited cost transparency in private/deployed mode
   - Pattern: customers on private deployments ask for token-level cost breakdowns per route and per model variant; current console reports aggregate GPU-hours only.
   - Impact: finance/engineering friction during capacity commit negotiations; some customers delaying scale-ups.

Representative quotes (verbatim / paraphrase):
- "We had a spike on Friday and half our calls timed out — we had to short-circuit to a smaller context. Cost us a day of rollback." — Platform lead, fintech customer.
- "Sometimes the model repeats a paragraph after a canary swap. Hard to tell if it's our prompt or the serving runtime." — ML infra engineer, healthcare customer.
- "We need to show our procurement team exact token cost per feature — the current monthly bill isn't granular enough." — Head of Data, mid-market SaaS.

Prioritized backlog (impact / effort shorthand: H/M/L):
- Fast win A: "prefetch-kv-on-canary" toggle (H impact / L effort) — server-side toggle to warm KV caches before increasing canary weight. Minimizes warmup spikes. Owner: SRE / serving-runtime. Jira: JIRA-3479.
- Fast win B: route-level token accounting in console (H impact / M effort) — add per-route token counters and 7-day trend view. Owner: product-console. Jira: JIRA-3501.
- Patch: improved replica cache invalidation hooks (H impact / M effort) — ensure deterministic cache eviction across replicas on rollout. Owner: serving-runtime. Jira: JIRA-3518.
- Medium: automated fallback policy simulator (M impact / M effort) — tool to simulate model-variant fallbacks with traffic profiles to predict duplication/latency effects. Owner: optimize team. Jira: JIRA-3599.
- Experiment: streaming-kernel-adaptive-swap (M impact / H effort) — spike to test partial-kernel swaps that avoid full fallback for long sequences. Owner: applied-ml + serving-runtime. Spike ticket: JIRA-3650.

Quick wins (detailed):
- Prefetch toggle: config flag at rollout controller to execute a small set of warmup requests (customer-provided short-prefixes) on new replicas before traffic shifts. Implementation: rollout-controller + small warmup worker; test: internal canary.
- Console token rows: add columns for "tokens_in", "tokens_out", "avg_latency_per_token" per route; wire to existing usage pipeline. Low UI surface, mostly data plumbing.
- Postmortem checklist update: add explicit KV-consistency validation after any model-variant rollout; owners must sign off before canary >20%.

Impact / complexity notes for eng partners:
- Prefetching is low-risk but requires safe handling of customer data (avoid storing warmup prefixes) — propose ephemeral warmup with scrubbed logs.
- Replica cache invalidation touches concurrency controls; low-level kernel changes may require regression harnesses. Allocate 2 sprints of QA.

Open questions / risks:
- Do we have legal/contract constraints on running customer-provided warmup prompts on shared infra? (legal + security check required)
- How representative are the warmup prefixes? Customers with variable conversation structure may still see misses.
- Telemetry: current trace sampling drops 80% of token-level traces — need a plan to increase sampling for rollout windows only.

Next steps / owners (short timeline):
- 2026-03-15: Kickoff implementation plan for prefetch toggle (owners: Jules Park, Carlos Mendes).
- 2026-03-22: Spec for route-level token accounting (owners: Priya Kapoor, Liam O'Neill).
- 2026-04-05: Start spike for replica invalidation correctness (owner: serving-runtime eng lead).
- PRs / tickets to create: JIRA-3479 (prefetch toggle), JIRA-3501 (route tokens), JIRA-3518 (cache eviction correctness).

Notes / scratch area (raw snippets from sources):
- Support ticket #99821: "latency climb on 10k token requests; resolved after instance restart" (linked to SRE incident 2025-09-04).
- Slack thread #cs-feedback: thread started by @audrey — includes a short screen recording showing token duplication after canary flip (timestamped).
- Interview note (Customer B): "We use rolling stateful sessions and can't afford duplicate responses — it's blocking our rollout to prod."

Unresolved:
- Which customers want the prefetch toggle by default vs opt-in? Need customer-segmentation run (CS to call top-12 impacted accounts).

Appendix: quick experiment checklist for CS to run with customers
1) Ask for a 30-min window to enable prefetch-warmup on a staging replica. Collect 100 sample requests.
2) Capture traces (enable high-sample mode for window).
3) Compare latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) and token duplication count.
4) Collate feedback and decide go/no-go.

If helpful, I'll convert this into a 1-pager for execs and a separate technical spec for the serving-runtime team.

---
Notes to self: this is intentionally compact — keep iterations in Drive, canonical spec moves to Confluence after initial dev signoffs.
